prod_011:n1.prompt:
You are helping me choose a status-page provider ({{vendor}}) for our public uptime commitment page. Before starting, ask me for: our primary domain, whether we need private/internal status pages (customer- or employee-specific access control) in addition to a public one, our approximate monthly incident/subscriber volume, our current monthly/annual budget ceiling for this tool, and any existing incident-management or monitoring tools we'd want it to integrate with.

Then do the following:
1. Research current status-page providers in the incident-management space, evaluating each against: (a) ability to run private/internal status pages with access control, (b) ability to publish a hosted public status page with custom domain support and subscriber notifications driven from incident state, (c) pricing tiers relative to my stated budget, (d) integration options with the tools I listed, and (e) ease of custom domain setup and branding.
2. Build a comparison table (provider, pricing tier, public+custom domain support, private/access-controlled pages, subscriber notification methods, key integrations, notable limitations).
3. Recommend a top 2-3 shortlist with a clear rationale tied to my stated needs and budget, noting trade-offs.
4. Draft a short summary I can review, including any account setup steps I'll need to complete (e.g., creating an account, choosing a plan, entering billing details).

Do not sign up for any service, enter payment information, or commit to a plan on my behalf — this remains a human step. Once your research and shortlist are ready, present the comparison table and recommendation, then stop for human sign-off so I can make the final vendor and billing decision.

prod_011:n2.prompt:
You are helping me set up public uptime monitoring for our status page using {{vendor}}, our chosen incident-management platform. I will give you our domain (e.g. status.ourdomain.com), the list of services/components we want tracked (e.g. API, Web App, Dashboard, Auth), and confirmation of our observability stack (Datadog, Grafana, Prometheus, CloudWatch, and/or Sentry) so you know which integrations to wire. If I haven't provided these, ask me for them before proceeding.

Please do the following using our configured credentials in {{vendor}}:
1. Create a component for each service/feature area we specify, naming them clearly and grouping related components if the platform supports grouping.
2. Set up uptime monitors for each component, either by connecting the relevant first-party integration (Datadog, Grafana, Prometheus, CloudWatch, or Sentry) per {{vendor}}'s documented setup, or by configuring a direct HTTP/ping check if no integration applies — ask me which method to use per component if it's unclear.
3. Map each monitor to its corresponding component so status changes automatically reflect component health.
4. Create (or configure) the public status page in {{vendor}}, enabling subscriber notifications (email/SMS/webhook as available) and preparing the custom domain setup (e.g. CNAME target) for status.ourdomain.com — note the DNS record details I'll need to add.
5. Verify each monitor is reporting data and each component displays the correct live status.

When done, report back: the list of components created, which monitors/integrations feed each one, the subscriber notification channels enabled, and the exact DNS record (type, host, value) I need to add to point our custom domain at the status page. Flag any component or integration you couldn't configure due to missing access or unclear requirements, and ask me for clarification rather than guessing.

prod_011:n3.prompt:
You are helping me publish our status page live on our own domain (e.g., status.yourdomain.com) using {{vendor}} as the edge platform. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for: (a) my root domain, (b) the subdomain I want the status page on (default to status.yourdomain.com if I don't specify), and (c) confirmation that my status page app/service is already built and ready to deploy (or ask where its source lives if not already deployed).

2. Using your configured credentials for {{vendor}}, deploy the status page application to {{vendor}}'s edge network via its CLI deploy command.

3. Attach the custom subdomain to the deployed service, and create/update the necessary DNS record (CNAME or equivalent) pointing the subdomain to the deployed service, using {{vendor}}'s dashboard or API.

4. Confirm that a free, auto-renewing TLS certificate is provisioned and active for the subdomain — check the certificate status via {{vendor}}'s dashboard or API rather than assuming.

5. Verify the page is reachable over HTTPS at the intended subdomain and that the certificate is valid (no browser warnings), and confirm DNS has propagated.

Done looks like: the status page loads over HTTPS at my chosen subdomain, served by {{vendor}}, with a valid auto-renewing TLS certificate and correct DNS routing in place.

Report back with: the final live URL, the DNS record type/value you created, confirmation of TLS certificate status, and any errors or propagation delays encountered. If anything requires me to approve billing, choose a plan, or make an account-level decision on {{vendor}}, list it clearly and stop for human sign-off.

prod_011:n4.prompt:
You are helping me draft a Service Level Agreement (SLA) document for my product, covering the uptime commitment and service credit terms. This is a content-drafting step only — no vendor integration or API calls are involved.

Before starting, ask me for anything you need that isn't already clear, such as: my company/product name, the domain the status page will live on, my target uptime percentage (e.g. 99.9%), the measurement period (monthly or quarterly), and any existing brand/legal tone preferences.

Then draft an SLA document that includes:
1. A clear uptime commitment statement (e.g. "We commit to 99.9% monthly uptime").
2. A definition of "downtime" or "unavailability" precise enough to be measured against the status page's uptime monitors.
3. A tiered service credit schedule — specify credit percentages or amounts tied to uptime shortfall ranges (e.g. below 99.9% = 10% credit, below 99.0% = 25% credit, etc.), using reasonable industry-standard tiers if I don't specify.
4. Exclusions (e.g. scheduled maintenance, force majeure, customer-caused outages).
5. The process customers must follow to request a credit, and any claim deadline.
6. Placeholder language noting this draft requires legal/counsel review before being finalized or included in contracts.

Format the draft as a clean, labeled document (plain text or markdown) I can hand to counsel and later insert into contracts and my status page.

When the draft is complete, present it to me in full along with a short summary of the key numbers chosen (uptime target, credit tiers, exclusions) and any assumptions you made. Do not send this draft to counsel or publish it anywhere — flag clearly that this draft still needs legal review and stop for human sign-off.

Report back with the full draft text and your summary of assumptions.

prod_011:n5.prompt:
You are helping me prepare the SLA credit terms for legal (counsel) review before we publish our status page and SLA. This is a policy-gate step: counsel must judge acceptable financial/liability exposure, so you must prepare everything needed for their review and then stop for human sign-off.

Please do the following:
1. Ask me for (if not already provided): our current draft SLA text or bullet points (uptime commitment %, measurement window, credit percentages per downtime tier, claim process/deadline, exclusions), our domain, the name/email of the attorney or law firm doing the review, and any prior counsel feedback.
2. Compile a clean, well-organized SLA credit-terms document (or update the existing draft) that clearly lays out: uptime targets, downtime tiers, credit percentages, how credits are calculated and capped, claim submission process, and exclusions.
3. Draft a concise cover email to counsel summarizing what needs review (specifically the credit percentages and triggers), any open questions we have, and a requested turnaround date.
4. Prepare a tracking note (e.g., in a doc or spreadsheet) logging: date sent, recipient, version of SLA sent, and a placeholder for their response/status, so we can poll for completion later.
5. Do NOT send the email or file anything on my behalf unless I explicitly ask you to send it using my configured credentials — and even then, do not approve, sign, or finalize any terms yourself.

When finished, stop for human sign-off and report back with: the finalized draft SLA credit-terms document, the drafted cover email, the tracking note, and a clear note that counsel's actual legal approval is a separate action I (or they) must complete manually — this decision remains a human step.

prod_011:n6.prompt:
You are helping me publish our finalized Service Level Agreement (SLA) into our contracts and our website. Before starting, ask me for anything you don't already have: (1) the final, counsel-approved SLA text including uptime commitment, measurement window, and credit terms; (2) my website's domain and the platform/CMS it runs on (e.g., a static site, WordPress, Webflow, etc.) and how you should access it (my configured credentials); (3) where our contract templates live and how they're managed (e.g., a document management or e-signature tool, or plain Word/Google Docs templates) and access details; (4) any legal-specific formatting requirements (defined terms, exhibit numbering, cross-references to the Master Services Agreement) counsel wants preserved.

Once you have these, do the following:
1. Add a new 'Service Level Agreement' or 'Uptime Commitment' page (or exhibit) to the website, linked clearly from the footer, pricing page, or trust/status page, using the approved SLA text exactly as provided.
2. Insert the SLA as a new exhibit or section into our standard contract template(s), matching existing formatting, numbering, and defined-terms conventions, and flag any inconsistencies you find between the SLA text and existing contract clauses (e.g., conflicting terms, notice periods).
3. Prepare a short summary of every file/page changed, with the exact diffs or before/after text, for my review.

Do not publish the website change live or send/execute any contract template changes without my review — prepare drafts, mark them clearly as pending, and then stop for human sign-off. Report back with: the list of files/pages touched, the draft text inserted in each, links or paths to review, and any flagged inconsistencies needing legal attention.
